# Weekly Multi-Asset Technology & Growth Market Briefing

The past week in markets was defined by a sharp and broad factor rotation away from long-duration growth, software, and higher-multiple innovators into cyclicals, legacy value, semiconductors at specific points in the stack, and select defensives. Within the watchlist, the dispersion between winners and losers was extreme, with several names posting moves of more than 20 percent over the week, both up and down, underscoring a regime where factor, liquidity, and positioning dynamics are dominating over single-name fundamentals. At a high level, semiconductors and select industrial and materials names such as Lumentum Holdings Inc. (LITE) up 40.9 percent on the week, Teradyne (TER) up 24.5 percent, Corning (GLW) up 18.3 percent, and Caterpillar (CAT) up 10.5 percent stood out on the upside, while high-multiple software, cybersecurity, health tech, and consumer internet significantly underperformed, with names such as Atlassian (TEAM) down 19.9 percent, Varonis (VRNS) down 24.1 percent, and Amplitude (AMPL) down 21.2 percent. The rotation occurred in an environment devoid of near-term earnings catalysts for the watchlist, suggesting macro, rates, and portfolio construction rather than fundamentals were the primary drivers.

## Market Overview

This week’s tape should be understood first and foremost as a continuation and intensification of a factor rotation that had already been building over the past month. Across the watchlist, the software complex and many high-duration growth names extended multi-week drawdowns, while a subset of cyclicals and specific hardware beneficiaries of secular themes such as AI and reshoring continued to grind higher. The month-on-month profile reinforces that these are not isolated moves: for example, on a one-month basis, TEAM is down 41.1 percent, Amplitude (AMPL) is down 37.9 percent, and HubSpot (HUBS) is down 41.6 percent, illustrating just how abrupt and violent the de-rating has been across even high-quality software franchises. In parallel, the one-month moves for names such as Western Digital (WDC), up 41.4 percent, Seagate (STX), up 39.3 percent, and GLW, up 38.8 percent, confirm a pronounced swing toward hardware, storage, and infrastructure proxies.

The rotation was also visible within megacap and hyperscaler exposure, which acted less as a safe haven and more as a funding source in the short term. Amazon (AMZN) declined 12.1 percent on the week and 12.9 percent over the month, Microsoft (MSFT) fell 6.8 percent week-on-week and 17.0 percent over the month, and Meta Platforms (META) was down 7.7 percent on the week even though it remains up 2.0 percent over the month. These moves suggest that investors are rebalancing away from crowded, AI-adjacent compounders in the near term, either to harvest gains, manage risk into macro uncertainty, or rotate into cheaper cyclicals and more narrowly defined AI hardware beneficiaries. At the same time, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) and other enabling semiconductor names held up relatively well, with TSM up 5.5 percent on the week and 9.5 percent on the month, underscoring an effort to remain levered to AI infrastructure while reducing exposure to more richly valued software layers.

The week was notably quiet from a micro-catalyst perspective. There are no watchlist earnings scheduled for the next two weeks, so price action was driven predominantly by cross-asset flows, macro repricing, and narrative shifts rather than company-specific news. The absence of earnings also means that multi-standard-deviation moves in either direction are more likely to reflect changes in discount rates, factor exposures, and positioning rather than hard changes to forward estimates. This is especially important when thinking about the software and cybersecurity drawdown, where the declines in many cases are outpacing any incremental fundamental deterioration that can be reasonably inferred from public information.

A further defining feature of the week was the renewed bifurcation within technology itself. Semiconductors were mixed but with pockets of very strong performance, led by LITE up 40.9 percent, TER up 24.5 percent, Arm Holdings (ARM) up 17.4 percent, and SiTime (SITM) up 15.3 percent. This contrasted sharply with other parts of the semiconductor space such as AMD, which fell 11.9 percent on the week and is roughly flat over the month, and IONQ, down 12.5 percent on the week and 29.7 percent on the month. The divergence reflects increasing discrimination between near-term earnings power and long-term optionality stories, as well as a re-rating of companies whose revenue visibility is increasingly tied to tangible AI infrastructure deployments.

Outside of technology, the strength in cyclicals, industrials, energy, and selected consumer staples continued to build. Names such as CNH Industrial (CNH), up 14.9 percent on the week and 24.9 percent on the month, Caterpillar (CAT), up 10.5 percent and 21.7 percent respectively, and Valero (VLO), up 11.7 percent and 10.2 percent, point to an environment in which investors are willing to pay for cyclical earnings leverage and real-asset exposure. Similarly, defensive staples and consumer names such as McCormick (MKC), up 9.0 percent on the week, Unilever (UL), up 5.5 percent on the week and 15.2 percent on the month, and Clorox (CLX), up 5.8 percent on the week and 17.3 percent on the month, have begun to act as ballast in multi-asset portfolios as volatility rises in growth and technology. This combination of cyclicals and defensives leading while software and speculative growth lag is characteristic of late-cycle or mid-cycle transitions where growth leadership pauses while investors reassess the durability of earnings in a potentially more volatile macro regime.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

Sector leadership during the week broke sharply against the grain of the prior multi-quarter trend, which had been dominated by hyperscalers, AI beneficiaries across the stack, and high-quality software. Within the watchlist, semiconductors and select hardware/storage names provided leadership, while software infrastructure, application software, cybersecurity, and ad tech/digital media became funding sources. The subsector bucket data makes this rotation particularly clear. In software infrastructure, every name in the bucket declined week-on-week except for DigitalOcean (DOCN), which rose 13.9 percent and 17.5 percent over the month. By contrast, Amplitude (AMPL) fell 21.2 percent on the week and 37.9 percent over the month, Datadog (DDOG) declined 13.6 percent on the week and 21.0 percent over the month, Snowflake (SNOW) fell 12.6 percent on the week and 27.9 percent on the month, and Dynatrace (DT) was down 11.5 percent and 23.1 percent over the week and month respectively. This juxtaposition suggests that investors are differentiating between smaller-cap, under-owned infrastructure providers with clearer paths to profitability or self-help stories such as DOCN, and larger, more fully valued observability and data platforms that had become consensus longs.

Application software fared even worse, signaling a market that is actively de-rating high-multiple, recurring-revenue models, particularly those exposed to discretionary IT budgets and seat-based pricing. Atlassian (TEAM) fell 19.9 percent on the week and 41.1 percent over the month, ServiceTitan (TTAN) declined 18.6 percent and 39.7 percent, Freshworks (FRSH) was down 17.2 percent and 25.2 percent, HubSpot (HUBS) declined 16.9 percent and 41.6 percent, Hims & Hers (HIMS) dropped 15.0 percent and 35.1 percent, monday.com (MNDY) was down 14.6 percent and 34.6 percent, Asana (ASAN) declined 14.5 percent and 35.3 percent, and ServiceNow (NOW) fell 13.9 percent and 33.2 percent over the week and month respectively. The breadth and magnitude of these declines across both SMB and enterprise-focused vendors indicate that the market is re-rating the entire cohort, likely in response to concerns about slowing net new ARR, longer sales cycles, pricing pressure, and the risk that AI-native workflows compress the value capture of traditional SaaS intermediaries.

Cybersecurity, which had been relatively defensive earlier in the year, also fell sharply, demonstrating that the market is no longer willing to pay peak multiples even for mission-critical categories when macro, rates, and positioning turn against long-duration growth. Varonis (VRNS) declined 24.1 percent on the week and 36.1 percent on the month, Zscaler (ZS) fell 16.3 percent and 27.6 percent, Qualys (QLYS) dropped 16.0 percent on both the weekly and monthly horizons, CrowdStrike (CRWD) was down 10.4 percent and 17.4 percent, Palo Alto Networks (PANW) fell 10.0 percent and 17.8 percent, Rapid7 (RPD) declined 9.3 percent and 26.0 percent, Rubrik (RBRK) fell 8.7 percent and 33.6 percent, and SentinelOne (S) declined 5.4 percent and 14.9 percent. The drawdown in VRNS is especially notable as the stock is now down over a third for the month, underscoring investor skepticism toward slower-growing, niche or legacy architectures within the broader security stack.

Within semiconductors, leadership rotated toward a different subset of names than in prior weeks, away from generic compute proxies and toward optics, testing, memory and storage, and timing. Lumentum (LITE) surged 40.9 percent on the week and 40.5 percent on the month, making it one of the best performers across the entire watchlist and signaling renewed optimism about optical components and 3D sensing demand. Teradyne (TER) gained 24.5 percent on the week and 34.9 percent on the month, reflecting strong expectations for semiconductor test demand as AI accelerators and advanced nodes scale. SiTime (SITM) rose 15.3 percent on the week and 22.2 percent on the month, likely benefiting from its leverage to precision timing solutions in high-speed data and communications infrastructure. Western Digital (WDC) and Seagate (STX), which sit at the intersection of storage, AI, and data center capex, climbed 12.9 percent and 5.3 percent on the week and an even stronger 41.4 percent and 39.3 percent on the month respectively, confirming that investors are increasingly looking down the stack from GPUs toward memory, storage, and connectivity as the next legs of the AI investment cycle.

By contrast, select semis with more speculative narratives or less near-term AI earnings leverage struggled. IonQ (IONQ), a quantum computing name with significant long-term optionality but limited current revenue scale, fell 12.5 percent on the week and 29.7 percent on the month. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) declined 11.9 percent on the week and is slightly negative at 0.8 percent on the month, despite remaining central to the AI and data center compute narrative, suggesting that some of the near-term enthusiasm and positioning had to reset. Credo Technology (CRDO) declined 11.1 percent on the week and 21.0 percent on the month, indicating that even connectivity beneficiaries are not immune when valuations get stretched or when supply-demand expectations become more uncertain. Synopsys (SNPS), a design automation and IP leader, also fell 8.2 percent on the week and 17.9 percent on the month, reflecting some de-rating of high-quality, but higher-multiple, EDA and IP franchises in the face of rising volatility.

AdTech and digital media further underlined the market’s newfound aversion to cyclical, advertising-sensitive, and identity-transitioning stories. Braze (BRZE) declined 14.6 percent on the week and 44.4 percent on the month, AppLovin (APP) fell 14.0 percent and 35.7 percent, Klaviyo (KVYO) dropped 13.8 percent and 35.6 percent, Pinterest (PINS) was down 11.4 percent and 28.7 percent, The Trade Desk (TTD) declined 10.8 percent and 30.0 percent, Omnicom (OMC) fell 9.3 percent and 9.9 percent, Zeta Global (ZETA) dropped 9.1 percent and 27.1 percent, and Sprinklr (CXM) declined 6.0 percent and 22.7 percent. The consistency of the drawdown across programmatic, marketing automation, and agency models suggests that investors are increasingly discounting the durability of digital ad demand amid macro uncertainty, as well as the potential cannibalization of traditional ad-tech stacks by large platforms’ AI-driven marketing suites.

In fintech, performance was more mixed, highlighting a nuanced re-evaluation of risk across payments, trading, consumer credit, and traditional financials. Coinbase (COIN) declined 15.2 percent on the week and 32.9 percent on the month, reflecting volatility in crypto asset prices and regulatory overhang. In contrast, BILL Holdings (BILL) rallied 13.4 percent on the week, though it remains down 13.1 percent on the month, which may indicate short-covering and bargain hunting after a prolonged drawdown. Block (XYZ) fell 7.4 percent on the week and 21.7 percent on the month, Affirm (AFRM) declined 5.4 percent and 31.3 percent, while more traditional financials including Bank of America (BAC) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) rose 6.3 percent and 5.4 percent respectively on the week, with BAC up 1.6 percent for the month and JPM modestly negative at 1.4 percent over the same period. Arch Capital (ACGL) also performed well, up 5.1 percent on the week and 6.1 percent on the month. The dispersion here supports a thesis of investors rotating from higher-risk fintech and consumer credit exposure into more capital-efficient, diversified financials and insurers that can benefit from a resilient rate backdrop and more stable credit conditions.

Consumer-facing names reflected a similarly bifurcated narrative. Shopify (SHOP) declined 14.6 percent on the week and 32.8 percent on the month, Wix (WIX) fell 13.2 percent and 24.6 percent, Global-E (GLBE) dropped 10.8 percent and 18.2 percent, and Sea Limited (SE) was down 6.8 percent and 22.1 percent, pointing to continued skepticism around e-commerce, cross-border trade, and emerging-market consumer demand. In contrast, staples and more defensive or value-oriented consumer names held up much better. McCormick (MKC) gained 9.0 percent on the week and 3.1 percent on the month, PVH rose 6.0 percent on the week and 0.2 percent on the month, Clorox (CLX) advanced 5.8 percent on the week and 17.3 percent on the month, and Five Below (FIVE) climbed 5.7 percent on the week and 1.0 percent on the month. This pattern aligns with a broader risk-off tilt within consumer, where investors are trimming high-multiple internet and GMV stories in favor of staples and value retailers.

Energy and industrials rounded out sector leadership. Within the Energy/Industrials bucket, Corning (GLW) surged 18.3 percent on the week and 38.8 percent on the month, Sable Offshore (SOC) declined 18.0 percent and 7.8 percent, CNH gained 14.9 percent and 24.9 percent, United Airlines (UAL) climbed 13.3 percent and is roughly flat at 0.6 percent down for the month, Kaiser Aluminum (KALU) advanced 13.0 percent and 12.8 percent, Valero (VLO) gained 11.7 percent and 10.2 percent, Eastman Chemical (EMN) rose 11.7 percent and 16.9 percent, and Mohawk Industries (MHK) gained 11.4 percent and 23.4 percent. The strength in these names suggests that investors are reasserting exposure to industrial production, travel, energy demand, and construction end-markets, possibly on expectations that global growth will prove more resilient than feared or that fiscal and industrial policy support will continue to backstop certain cyclical areas.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

Even in a week dominated by macro and factor dynamics, several individual names on the watchlist posted moves that warrant closer examination from a risk and positioning standpoint. Among the most notable upside movers, Lumentum (LITE) stood out with a 40.9 percent gain on the week and 40.5 percent on the month, effectively re-rating the stock higher in response to a combination of improved sentiment around optical demand, cost actions, and perhaps rising investor conviction that AI data center and 3D sensing opportunities can re-ignite growth. From a portfolio construction perspective, the magnitude and speed of this move raise questions about entry points and risk-reward from here, especially given the inherently cyclical nature of optical components and the dependency on a relatively small set of large customers.

Teradyne (TER) was another key outperformer, gaining 24.5 percent on the week and 34.9 percent over the month. As a leading provider of semiconductor test equipment, Teradyne sits in a sweet spot of the AI value chain, benefiting from rising complexity, tighter process tolerances, and expanding test content per device as AI accelerators and advanced nodes proliferate. The strong performance signals that investors are increasingly willing to look beyond near-term cyclicality in chip capex toward the structural demand created by AI, 5G, and advanced packaging. However, this also introduces the risk of crowding and heightened sensitivity to any slowdown in foundry or fabless spending intentions.

Corning (GLW) gained 18.3 percent on the week and 38.8 percent on the month, making it one of the strongest non-semiconductor performers in the watchlist. As a specialty materials leader with exposure to display glass, optical fiber, and other high-performance materials, Corning benefits from multiple secular drivers including data center interconnect, broadband deployment, and advanced displays. The stock’s multi-week strength implies a shift in investor perception, from viewing Corning as a relatively mature cyclical to viewing it as a key enabler of the bandwidth and connectivity layers underpinning AI and cloud infrastructure. This re-rating also narrows the valuation gap with more obviously AI-linked hardware and infrastructure names, but it leaves less room for error in execution or macro conditions.

Western Digital (WDC) and Seagate (STX) together highlight the market’s renewed focus on storage as a critical bottleneck and beneficiary of AI and big data workloads. WDC gained 12.9 percent on the week and 41.4 percent on the month, while STX rose 5.3 percent on the week and 39.3 percent on the month. Both companies are leveraged to higher-capacity drives and enterprise storage demand, and recent price action suggests that investors are increasingly comfortable underwriting a multi-year upgrade cycle as AI workloads require larger, faster, and more resilient storage architectures. These moves may also reflect expectations of a more favorable pricing environment and tighter supply after a prolonged downturn in the memory and storage cycle.

On the downside, the most dramatic drawdowns were concentrated in software, cybersecurity, and certain health and life sciences names. Varonis (VRNS) declined 24.1 percent on the week and 36.1 percent on the month, making it one of the weakest names in the entire watchlist. This scale of drawdown typically signals a combination of multiple compression and rising concerns around growth durability, competitive intensity, or product relevance. In the absence of fresh earnings data, the price action suggests that investors are questioning the extent to which Varonis’s data security and governance offerings can command premium growth and margins in an increasingly crowded security landscape, especially as customers rationalize vendors and shift toward platform-based security strategies.

Amplitude (AMPL) declined 21.2 percent on the week and 37.9 percent on the month, underscoring the vulnerability of analytics and product-led growth tools to both macro headwinds and evolving AI-native competition. As a provider of product analytics, Amplitude sits at the intersection of digital product development and customer engagement. However, the stock’s steep drawdown suggests that investors fear decelerating demand, increased competitive pressure from more horizontally integrated platforms, and potential disruption as AI-enabled analytics and experimentation tools become more pervasive. The magnitude of the decline relative to the available fundamental information implies that positioning and liquidity may also be important drivers.

Atlassian (TEAM) fell 19.9 percent on the week and 41.1 percent on the month, extending a sharp de-rating that has swept across premium collaboration and workflow software. Meanwhile, HubSpot (HUBS) declined 16.9 percent on the week and 41.6 percent on the month, marking an even more severe multiple compression for a company that had been viewed as a category leader in marketing and CRM for SMBs and mid-market customers. These moves reflect both top-down and bottom-up concerns. Top-down, they reflect the market’s broader skepticism about the durability of high growth rates at premium multiples. Bottom-up, they encode worries that customers may slow seat expansion, rationalize tool stacks, and look to bundled offerings from larger platforms, while AI-enabled automation reduces the need for manual workflows and traditional seat-based licenses.

Another notable underperformer was Novo Nordisk (NVO), which fell 19.8 percent on the week and 15.8 percent on the month despite remaining a central player in the GLP-1 and metabolic disease narrative. The decline suggests that even category leaders in structurally growing end-markets are not immune to profit-taking, regulatory concerns, and expectations of intensifying competition, particularly when valuations are rich. For multi-asset portfolios with exposure to large-cap pharma and obesity drugs, the move in NVO may prompt a re-examination of position sizing, diversification across therapeutic areas, and risk-reward balance given policy and competitive uncertainties.

IQVIA (IQV) declined 18.5 percent on the week and 23.2 percent on the month, signaling investor concerns around the life sciences services and data ecosystem. IQVIA’s drawdown may capture worries about biopharma funding conditions, regulatory scrutiny, and the margin impact of AI and automation reshaping clinical trial and data services. The move also raises questions about the resilience of the broader life sciences tools and services complex, as Thermo Fisher (TMO) also fell 6.2 percent on the week and 12.0 percent on the month, while IQV’s downturn is more severe.

Within fintech and crypto-exposed names, Coinbase (COIN) declined 15.2 percent on the week and 32.9 percent on the month, underscoring the sensitivity of trading volumes, fee pools, and equity valuations to crypto asset price volatility and regulatory developments. At the same time, Block (XYZ) fell 7.4 percent on the week and 21.7 percent on the month, and Affirm (AFRM) declined 5.4 percent on the week and 31.3 percent on the month, signaling that the market is actively re-pricing higher-risk, consumer-oriented fintech business models. These dynamics may improve the risk-reward of more diversified and capital-efficient financials such as BAC, which gained 6.3 percent on the week and 1.6 percent on the month, and JPM, which rose 5.4 percent on the week.

It is important to emphasize that there were no watchlist earnings during the week and none are scheduled for the next two weeks. As such, the moves discussed above are best interpreted through the lens of factor exposures, valuations, and macro narratives rather than idiosyncratic earnings surprises, guidance changes, or company-specific shocks. This increases the risk of overshooting in both directions and suggests that fundamental investors should focus on distinguishing between pure multiple compression and genuine shifts in medium-term earnings power.

## Macro & Rates Environment

While no specific macro data prints are enumerated here, the behavior of equities, sector rotations, and style factor performance offer important clues about the prevailing macro and rates environment. The strong relative performance of cyclical industrials, energy, and certain materials such as CAT, CNH, VLO, EMN, and MHK, along with the resilience of diversified banks like BAC and JPM, suggests that markets are not pricing in an imminent deep recession. Instead, the pattern is more consistent with an environment of still-reasonable growth expectations, but with increasing concern around the impact of rates, inflation, and policy on long-duration assets and high-multiple growth equities.

The pronounced de-rating across software and high-growth technology is consistent with a backdrop in which real yields remain elevated relative to the prior decade, and where the path of policy rates is seen as higher for longer than the market had once assumed. In such an environment, the present value of long-dated cash flows is more heavily discounted, which disproportionately affects categories like application software, analytics, and certain fintech and health tech businesses. The steep one-month declines in TEAM, HUBS, NOW, MNDY, and others underscore this effect, as these companies had historically been afforded premium multiples based on strong growth and recurring revenue, but now face a new valuation regime in which investors demand greater profitability and capital efficiency.

The divergence within technology and growth also speaks to the market’s attempt to reconcile secular AI optimism with cyclical and valuation constraints. Hardware, semiconductors, and infrastructure names that can show tangible revenue and earnings uplift from AI deployments, such as LITE, TER, WDC, STX, and TSM, have been relatively better positioned. Their strong weekly and monthly performance indicates that investors are willing to maintain, or even increase, exposure to AI, but are rotating along the stack toward areas where the earnings inflection is sooner, more visible, and more directly tied to physical deployments of compute and storage. Software names that are still in the narrative phase of AI adoption without clear monetization pathways are more exposed to de-rating as investors re-underwrite their long-term assumptions.

The strength in energy names such as VLO and DVN, which gained 11.7 percent and 8.9 percent on the week and 10.2 percent and 27.1 percent on the month respectively, and in industrials such as CAT, CNH, FIX, and VMI, suggests expectations of sustained demand for commodities, infrastructure, and industrial capacity. DVN’s 27.1 percent one-month gain and KALU’s 12.8 percent one-month return are consistent with narratives of tight supply in certain commodities, structural underinvestment in upstream capacity, and ongoing demand linked to data center, energy transition, and industrial policy. Meanwhile, power and utilities-adjacent names like Generac (GNRC), up 9.2 percent on the week and 29.4 percent on the month, and GE Vernova (GEV), up 7.3 percent on the week and 17.7 percent on the month, highlight how electrification, grid modernization, and data center power demand are evolving into core investment themes.

Defensives and staples have begun to act more like protection in multi-asset portfolios. The multi-week strength in CLX, UL, MKC, and GIS (with UL up 15.2 percent and CLX up 17.3 percent over the month) reflects a rotation toward companies with pricing power, stable cash flows, and lower economic sensitivity. This is characteristic of environments in which investors seek to preserve capital amid volatility in higher-beta sectors, or where inflation and policy uncertainties raise the appeal of companies that can pass through costs and maintain margins.

The behavior of financials is another window into macro and rates sentiment. BAC and JPM’s gains of 6.3 percent and 5.4 percent on the week, combined with a positive one-month return for BAC, suggest that the yield curve and credit environment are seen as manageable from a bank earnings standpoint, with net interest margins and credit quality not deteriorating as quickly as feared. LPL Financial (LPLA), up 5.7 percent on the week and 7.2 percent on the month, reflects healthy demand for advisory and wealth management services, whereas more speculative fintech and crypto-exposed names such as COIN and AFRM have underperformed sharply, indicating risk aversion at the higher end of the risk spectrum.

Without near-term central bank or macro event risk explicitly embedded in the watchlist data, the appropriate conclusion is that the macro and rates environment remains a critical, but indirect, driver of performance. Investors appear to be repositioning for a world where growth is still positive but more volatile, inflation is stickier than pre-pandemic norms, and policy rates remain above the ultra-low levels that supported the last decade’s bull market in duration-heavy growth assets. In that world, portfolio construction requires a more balanced exposure across growth, value, cyclicals, and defensives, with a greater emphasis on cash generation, balance sheet strength, and pricing power.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Lumentum Holdings Inc. (LITE)

Lumentum’s 40.9 percent gain on the week and 40.5 percent gain on the month catapult it into the top tier of watchlist performers and demands a deeper examination of the underlying drivers. Lumentum operates in optical communications and commercial lasers, with exposure to telecom, data centers, and 3D sensing. The magnitude of the recent move suggests that investors are reassessing the company’s role in enabling high-bandwidth connectivity and sensing for AI data centers and advanced devices. It likely reflects improving sentiment around carrier and cloud capex, early signs of normalization in demand after a cyclical downturn, and potential upside from new design wins in AI-related optical modules and coherent systems.

From a positioning standpoint, the speed of the re-rating creates both opportunities and risks. On one hand, Lumentum’s end-market exposures align well with the medium-term demand outlook for fiber optics, high-speed interconnects, and 3D sensing, all of which are critical to supporting the growth of AI workloads and edge computing. On the other hand, the stock now embeds an expectation of sustained improvement, making it more sensitive to any wobble in orders, pricing, or competitive dynamics. Portfolio managers should consider whether to treat Lumentum as a tactical trade on improving optical cycles and AI-related demand, or as a more strategic core holding in the AI infrastructure value chain.

### Teradyne, Inc. (TER)

Teradyne’s 24.5 percent weekly gain and 34.9 percent monthly advance underscore the market’s conviction that semiconductor test is a key beneficiary of the AI and advanced node transition. As chips become more complex, with higher transistor counts, 3D architectures, and heterogeneous integration, the test content per device and the sophistication of test equipment increase. Teradyne is positioned to capture this growth, particularly in system-on-chip and memory test, as well as in emerging applications such as automotive and industrial semiconductors.

The recent performance likely reflects a combination of improved visibility into test demand, positive commentary from customers and ecosystem partners, and a re-rating toward premium multiples for companies that are seen as essential enablers of AI and high-performance compute. The challenge from here will be managing expectations: the stock’s strong run raises the bar for future orders and earnings, and any signs of pushouts in capex or slower-than-expected adoption of advanced test solutions could trigger volatility. For long-term investors, Teradyne remains a high-quality levered play on semiconductor complexity, but position sizing should account for the cyclical nature of chip capex and the risk of shorter-term corrections after such a sharp move.

### Western Digital Corporation (WDC)

Western Digital’s 12.9 percent gain on the week and 41.4 percent surge over the month highlight the market’s shifting focus toward storage as a bottleneck in AI and big data architectures. WDC is exposed to both hard disk drives and flash storage, serving hyperscalers, enterprises, and consumers. The stock’s recent strength suggests investor confidence that pricing in NAND and HDD is improving from cyclical troughs and that demand for high-capacity drives and enterprise SSDs will accelerate as AI workloads proliferate.

The key debate now revolves around how durable this storage upcycle will prove, and how quickly WDC can convert higher pricing and volumes into margin expansion and free cash flow. The stock’s strong run narrows the margin of safety for new capital, but it also reflects a recalibration from depressed levels during the downcycle. For diversified portfolios, WDC can serve as a targeted way to express a bullish view on AI-driven data growth and data center capex without owning GPUs directly. Risk factors include the usual storage cycle risks, competitive pressures, and the potential for new technologies to alter the mix between NAND, HDD, and other storage solutions.

### Corning Incorporated (GLW)

Corning’s 18.3 percent weekly gain and 38.8 percent monthly performance position it as a key stealth beneficiary of AI and digital infrastructure. Corning’s portfolio spans display glass, optical fiber and cable, automotive glass, and specialty materials. The stock’s recent strength likely reflects improved expectations for optical fiber demand as network operators and hyperscalers invest in higher-bandwidth connectivity to support AI, as well as a recovery in display and other industrial end-markets.

For investors, Corning offers a differentiated way to access AI and digital infrastructure without the cyclicality of semiconductors or the concentration risk of a few large cloud providers. Its materials technology and intellectual property create a competitive moat, while its diversified end-market exposure provides some resilience. However, the stock’s re-rating raises questions about valuation versus growth, and whether the company can consistently deliver above-market growth and margin expansion. Monitoring order trends, capex plans of major carriers and cloud providers, and the pace of adoption of new optical technologies will be critical.

### Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN)

Amazon’s 12.1 percent decline on the week and 12.9 percent slide over the month stand in contrast to its prior leadership and the broader AI enthusiasm. Amazon remains a core hyperscaler and cloud infrastructure provider through AWS, a dominant e-commerce player, and an emerging force in digital advertising. The recent drawdown suggests a combination of profit-taking, rotation out of crowded megacap growth, and some investor concern about the durability of margin expansion across retail, cloud, and ads in an evolving macro environment.

From a fundamental perspective, Amazon’s long-term thesis remains anchored in its scale advantages, diversified revenue streams, and ability to monetize AI both within AWS and across consumer-facing products. The market’s current de-rating may reflect higher discount rates and a desire to rebalance away from big tech concentration, rather than a structural shift in Amazon’s competitive position. For long-term portfolios, the key question is whether the recent move offers an attractive entry point relative to intrinsic value and growth, or whether further de-rating is likely if macro or regulatory headwinds intensify. Risk management considerations include position size relative to index exposure and the correlation of AMZN with other large-cap tech holdings.

### Microsoft Corporation (MSFT)

Microsoft’s 6.8 percent weekly decline and 17.0 percent monthly drawdown highlight a similar de-risking dynamic within hyperscalers and AI platform leaders. Microsoft has been at the center of the AI narrative through its partnership with OpenAI and the integration of AI across Azure, Office, and other products. The recent price action, however, indicates that even the highest-quality compounders are not immune when investors re-evaluate valuations and factor exposures.

The drawdown may represent a reset in expectations after a period of intense AI-driven optimism and multiple expansion. While the company’s fundamentals remain strong, and its strategic positioning in cloud, enterprise software, and AI is arguably unmatched, the market’s risk appetite for long-duration growth at elevated multiples appears to be more constrained. This underscores Meta’s scale advantages and the relative safety of platform-based models compared with more narrowly focused ad-tech intermediaries. The recent re-rating does, however, raise questions about how much of the upturn is already priced in and how sensitive these names will be to any slowdown in global growth or commodity demand. Monitoring order backlogs, pricing, and regional demand trends will be key.

## Upcoming Catalysts

While the precomputed data indicate that there are no watchlist earnings in the next two weeks, several categories of catalysts remain relevant for the coming period. First, macro data releases and central bank communications will continue to shape the trajectory of rates, inflation expectations, and risk appetite. These in turn will influence the relative performance of long-duration growth versus value, cyclicals versus defensives, and financials versus more speculative fintech. In particular, any data points that alter the expected path of policy rates could have outsized impacts on software, high-multiple technology, and real-asset sectors.

Second, sector-specific news flow and industry data points can act as important catalysts even in the absence of company-specific earnings. For semiconductors, updates from foundries, equipment makers, and large end-customers on AI-driven capex, node transitions, and supply-demand balances will be critical for names like TER, TSM, AMD, INTC, LITE, and WDC. Any indication of acceleration or deceleration in AI-related investment could lead to significant repricing across the value chain. Similarly, for storage and data center infrastructure names such as STX, VRT, and GLW, announcements related to hyperscaler capex plans, data center buildouts, and power and cooling constraints will be closely watched.

Third, regulatory and policy developments in areas such as digital assets, cybersecurity, healthcare pricing, and tech regulation may serve as important catalysts. For COIN and other crypto-exposed names, regulatory actions and guidance remain central drivers of sentiment and business model viability. For cybersecurity names like CRWD, PANW, ZS, and VRNS, regulatory requirements around data protection, critical infrastructure, and cyber resilience can influence demand and competitive dynamics. For healthcare and pharma, including NVO and ABT, policy debates around drug pricing, reimbursement, and safety can move valuations materially.

Fourth, competitive dynamics and product announcements across software, AI, and digital platforms can significantly shift sentiment. Launches of new AI models, platform capabilities, or pricing changes by hyperscalers such as AMZN, MSFT, and GOOG can impact the perceived value and bargaining power of downstream software vendors. If large platforms increasingly bundle AI capabilities into core suites, this could exert pressure on smaller, point-solution vendors across analytics, collaboration, and marketing tech, affecting names like AMPL, SNOW, DDOG, TEAM, BRZE, and KVYO.

Finally, positioning and technical factors may themselves act as catalysts. With many software and growth names already de-rated significantly over the past month, any stabilization in macro or rates could trigger short-covering and mean reversion. Conversely, continued inflows into value, cyclicals, and defensives could extend the current rotation. Monitoring flows, factor performance, and short interest will help gauge whether the recent moves have overshot fundamentals and whether the risk-reward is shifting.

## What To Watch Next Week

In the coming week, investors should focus on whether the factor rotation away from software and long-duration growth and toward semiconductors, industrials, energy, and defensives persists, accelerates, or begins to mean-revert. The magnitude of the one-month moves—such as TEAM down 41.1 percent, HUBS down 41.6 percent, BRZE down 44.4 percent, and NVO down 15.8 percent—suggests that positioning has been materially altered, and that some of the valuation excesses in high-growth names have been cleared. This creates the conditions for potential stabilization or even tactical bounces if macro data or policy signals are not incrementally negative.

On the positive side, the durability of gains in names like LITE, TER, WDC, STX, GLW, CAT, CNH, DVN, and VLO will be a key test of the market’s conviction in the AI infrastructure, industrial, and energy narratives. If these names hold their recent advances or continue to grind higher, it would suggest that investors are incrementally more confident in a soft-landing or mid-cycle reacceleration scenario, and in the structural nature of AI and infrastructure demand. Any abrupt reversals, by contrast, might signal that recent moves were driven more by short-term positioning than by a durable thesis.

In software and cybersecurity, the primary question is whether the recent drawdown marks the beginning of a prolonged de-rating or a sharp but ultimately transient reset. The breadth of declines across AMPL, SNOW, DDOG, TEAM, NOW, HUBS, ZS, CRWD, and PANW indicates that the sector has fallen out of favor at a factor level. However, the underlying businesses remain critical to digital transformation and security, and secular demand drivers have not disappeared. Investors should watch for signs of incremental stabilization in these stocks, such as smaller daily drawdowns, constructive reactions to even modestly positive news, or relative strength versus broader indices.

In fintech and consumer, monitoring the behavior of COIN, XYZ, AFRM, SHOP, WIX, GLBE, and SE will be important for gauging risk appetite toward higher-beta, consumer and transaction-driven business models. Stronger performance in diversified financials like BAC, JPM, LPLA, and ACGL may continue if rates and credit conditions remain supportive, while further weakness in crypto and consumer fintech would confirm a more enduring shift toward higher-quality financial exposures.

Across the broader watchlist, attention should be paid to any emerging divergences within sectors that could signal changing competitive dynamics or investor preferences. For example, within semiconductors, whether AMD and IONQ can stabilize relative to LITE, TER, and TSM will shed light on the market’s appetite for longer-duration AI optionality versus near-term earnings leverage. Within consumer, the performance gap between staples like UL, CLX, MKC, and discretionary or e-commerce names such as SHOP and FIVE will inform views on consumer strength and inflation pass-through.

Finally, from a top-down perspective, the week ahead will test whether markets can digest recent volatility and rotation without spilling over into a broader risk-off episode. If macro data and policy communications are broadly in line with expectations, there is scope for a stabilization of growth and technology names at lower multiples and for a more orderly leadership transition. However, any negative surprises on growth, inflation, or policy could exacerbate the pressure on long-duration assets and extend the advantage for value, cyclicals, and defensives.

## Conclusion

This week’s market action across the watchlist underscores a critical inflection point in the current cycle, with a decisive rotation away from high-multiple software, speculative growth, and certain AI-adjacent narratives and toward semiconductors, industrials, energy, storage, and defensives. The dispersion of returns has been extreme, with names like LITE up 40.9 percent and TER up 24.5 percent on the week, while VRNS, AMPL, and TEAM fell more than 20 percent in the same period. Over the month, many high-quality software and marketing tech names have seen their market capitalizations reduced by a third or more, while storage, specialty materials, and industrials have rallied by 20–40 percent.

In this environment, the central task for buy-side investors is to differentiate between moves driven primarily by changes in discount rates and factor exposures, and those that reflect genuine shifts in medium-term earnings power and competitive position. For many software and cybersecurity names, the recent drawdown appears to be more about valuation reset and macro-driven risk aversion than about structural impairment. Conversely, for semiconductors, storage, and certain industrial and energy names, the recent strength reflects a combination of cyclical recovery and structural demand tied to AI, infrastructure, and energy transition, but also introduces the risk of crowding and elevated expectations.

Portfolio construction should adapt to this new regime by balancing exposure to secular growth themes such as AI and digital transformation with increased emphasis on cash generation, capital discipline, and valuation support. This may involve rotating within sectors—from weaker, more speculative names into higher-quality leaders at more attractive entry points—rather than abandoning entire themes. It may also involve increasing allocations to industrials, energy, defensives, and selected financials to improve diversification and reduce sensitivity to higher rates and macro volatility.

Looking ahead, the absence of near-term earnings catalysts on the watchlist means that macro, policy, and factor dynamics will continue to dominate short-term price action. This raises the risk of further overshooting but also creates opportunities for fundamentally driven investors to add to high-conviction names at more reasonable valuations. Close monitoring of macro data, rates, sector-specific indicators, and competitive developments will be essential to navigate the coming weeks. In the meantime, maintaining a disciplined, balanced, and valuation-aware approach is likely to be the most effective way to manage risk and capture opportunities in a market that is rapidly repricing the relative value of growth, value, and cyclicals.

risks.risk: Re-acceleration in inflation and higher-for-longer Fed path
risks.impact: A string of hotter CPI prints and oil hovering near multi-month highs risks embedding a higher inflation regime into expectations. If markets conclude that the Fed must keep rates elevated or even hike further, long-duration assets such as high-growth software, unprofitable tech, and crypto-linked equities could face renewed multiple compression and volatility, while financial conditions tighten more broadly for corporates and consumers alike. This would likely favor value, cash-generating cyclicals, and energy over high-multiple growth, and increase downside tail risks for indices heavily concentrated in mega-cap tech. It also raises the bar for earnings to offset valuation pressure, making each upcoming inflation and labor data release a key volatility event for equities and rates-sensitive sectors alike. If inflation fails to moderate, defensive positioning in quality balance sheets and shorter-duration assets may outperform as investors seek resilience over pure growth exposure. The equity risk premium could be pressured further, lowering the cushion for any macro or earnings disappointment as real yields stay elevated and cash remains a compelling alternative for incremental capital allocation. Higher volatility around macro prints would likely keep systematic and options-driven flows in focus for short-term market dynamics, particularly in crowded AI and software trades where positioning is still extended despite the pullback. A prolonged higher-for-longer stance may also begin to pressure housing, credit-sensitive consumption, and weaker balance sheets, potentially widening performance dispersion within consumer and financials sectors over the coming quarters. The interaction between inflation, oil, and geopolitical risks in the Middle East will therefore remain central to both top-down and bottom-up equity risk management as we move deeper into the year, with portfolio hedging and sector tilts increasingly calibrated to alternative inflation scenarios and rate paths rather than a smooth glide toward the Fed’s target. Over time, sustained inflation overshoots could also force a reassessment of long-term margin assumptions in sectors with limited pricing power, amplifying valuation risk where earnings are back-end loaded and highly sensitive to cost structures and wage dynamics rather than near-term demand trends. As such, keeping close watch on forward inflation expectations, breakevens, and wage indicators will be critical for adjusting risk exposures in a timely manner as the macro narrative evolves. The balance between cyclical growth support from strong employment and the inflationary impulse it generates will likely dictate whether indices can continue to grind higher or face a more pronounced consolidation phase into the second half of the year. A regime of choppy, data-dependent trading is therefore the base case, with asymmetric downside around negative surprises in inflation or inflation-sensitive data such as oil, rents, and wage growth. Investors may increasingly look to barbell portfolios that combine structural growth themes like AI with inflation beneficiaries in energy, commodities, and value financials to navigate this environment. Over the near term, positioning and sentiment could amplify moves around each CPI release as markets test the Fed’s tolerance for inflation noise versus trend and the probability of policy error on either side of the mandate. In that context, risk management discipline around macro event risk becomes as important as stock selection in driving total returns across equity portfolios. Ultimately, the path of inflation remains the single most important macro swing factor for U.S. equity multiples and cross-asset correlations over the next several quarters, warranting sustained attention in both strategic and tactical asset allocation decisions. A failure of inflation to normalize would likely keep volatility structurally higher and prevent a decisive rotation back into the most duration-sensitive parts of the growth complex, even if earnings remain solid at the index level. Conversely, any credible sign of disinflation resuming could unlock a powerful catch-up rally in beaten-down software and long-duration tech, rewarding investors who have maintained optionality in these areas despite near-term drawdowns. For now, however, the balance of risks around inflation is skewed toward a more patient Fed and a cautious market stance on the timing and depth of any future easing cycle, keeping pressure on the most richly valued segments of the equity market. Maintaining flexibility and avoiding over-concentration in a single macro outcome remains prudent for portfolio construction in this uncertain environment. As a result, multi-asset investors are likely to continue balancing equity risk with allocations to cash, high-quality credit, and real assets that can help offset inflation and interest-rate shocks. Over time, the market’s ability to adapt to a higher nominal and real yield environment will be a key determinant of whether current equity valuations can be sustained without a more material reset in prices or earnings expectations, particularly in growth-heavy indices. In sum, inflation risk remains central to equity strategy and warrants close monitoring of both macro data and policy communication. The next several inflation prints will thus carry outsized importance for setting the tone into year-end and will likely dictate whether recent volatility in growth and AI sectors is a brief shakeout or the start of a more durable style rotation. Investors should remain nimble and prepared for elevated cross-asset correlations and factor swings around each major data release in this context. Maintaining diversification across styles, sectors, and duration profiles remains a key risk management tool as the inflation and policy narrative continues to evolve. A disciplined approach to scenario analysis and stress testing can help illuminate portfolio vulnerabilities to adverse inflation outcomes and guide proactive adjustments before market volatility forces reactive moves. As such, inflation and the Fed’s response function remain at the top of the equity risk radar for the foreseeable future. A careful balance between offense in structurally attractive growth areas and defense in inflation beneficiaries and quality cyclicals is likely to define successful positioning in this phase of the cycle. Continued vigilance on the interaction between inflation, growth, and policy will be critical for navigating what remains a complex and fluid macro backdrop for U.S. equities. A failure to adequately account for inflation risk could result in unexpected drawdowns, particularly in crowded trades where valuations and positioning leave little margin for error. Maintaining a forward-looking perspective on inflation dynamics and their implications for earnings, multiples, and cross-asset flows will thus remain central to effective equity risk management. In short, inflation is both the key risk and the key potential catalyst for a shift in market leadership over the coming quarters. A renewed disinflation trend could re-energize growth and AI leaders, while persistent inflation would favor value, real assets, and shorter-duration exposures. The market’s ongoing tug-of-war between these scenarios underpins much of the current volatility and style rotation, making inflation data the critical swing factor for equity strategy at this juncture. A nuanced view that incorporates both macro and micro drivers will be essential for navigating this environment successfully. Investors should stay engaged but selective, focusing on quality and resilience while retaining optionality to capitalize on potential shifts in the inflation and policy narrative. The current backdrop demands heightened attention to both top-down risks and bottom-up fundamentals. A disciplined, diversified approach remains the best defense against the uncertainties surrounding inflation and the Fed’s next steps. Over time, the market’s resolution of this inflation debate will likely set the stage for the next durable phase of equity leadership and performance. Until then, flexibility, diversification, and risk-aware positioning are paramount for equity investors. Maintaining a balanced and dynamic stance toward inflation risk is, therefore, critical for protecting capital and capturing opportunities in the evolving market landscape. Ultimately, how inflation evolves will define the winners and losers across sectors, styles, and individual securities in the period ahead. A robust framework for monitoring and responding to inflation data will be a key differentiator for successful equity investing in this environment. Inflation, in short, remains the central macro risk and opportunity set for U.S. equities today. In that context, careful calibration of risk exposures to different inflation outcomes will continue to be a core task for investors. The coming months will likely provide important clarity on this front as new data and policy decisions unfold. risks.detail: A string of hotter CPI prints and oil hovering near multi-month highs risks embedding a higher inflation regime into expectations. If markets conclude that the Fed must keep rates elevated or even hike further, long-duration assets such as high-growth software, unprofitable tech, and crypto-linked equities could face renewed multiple compression and volatility, while financial conditions tighten more broadly for corporates and consumers alike. This would likely favor value, cash-generating cyclicals, and energy over high-multiple growth, and increase downside tail risks for indices heavily concentrated in mega-cap tech. It also raises the bar for earnings to offset valuation pressure, making each upcoming inflation and labor data release a key volatility event for equities and rates-sensitive sectors alike. If inflation fails to moderate, defensive positioning in quality balance sheets and shorter-duration assets may outperform as investors seek resilience over pure growth exposure. The equity risk premium could be pressured further, lowering the cushion for any macro or earnings disappointment as real yields stay elevated and cash remains a compelling alternative for incremental capital allocation. Higher volatility around macro prints would likely keep systematic and options-driven flows in focus for short-term market dynamics, particularly in crowded AI and software trades where positioning is still extended despite the pullback. A prolonged higher-for-longer stance may also begin to pressure housing, credit-sensitive consumption, and weaker balance sheets, potentially widening performance dispersion within consumer and financials sectors over the coming quarters. The interaction between inflation, oil, and geopolitical risks in the Middle East will therefore remain central to both top-down and bottom-up equity risk management as we move deeper into the year, with portfolio hedging and sector tilts increasingly calibrated to alternative inflation scenarios and rate paths rather than a smooth glide toward the Fed’s target. Over time, sustained inflation overshoots could also force a reassessment of long-term margin assumptions in sectors with limited pricing power, amplifying valuation risk where earnings are back-end loaded and highly sensitive to cost structures and wage dynamics rather than near-term demand trends. As such, keeping close watch on forward inflation expectations, breakevens, and wage indicators will be critical for adjusting risk exposures in a timely manner as the macro narrative evolves. The balance between cyclical growth support from strong employment and the inflationary impulse it generates will likely dictate whether indices can continue to grind higher or face a more pronounced consolidation phase into the second half of the year. A regime of choppy, data-dependent trading is therefore the base case, with asymmetric downside around negative surprises in inflation or inflation-sensitive data such as oil, rents, and wage growth. Investors may increasingly look to barbell portfolios that combine structural growth themes like AI with inflation beneficiaries in energy, commodities, and value financials to navigate this environment. Over the near term, positioning and sentiment could amplify moves around each CPI release as markets test the Fed’s tolerance for inflation noise versus trend and the probability of policy error on either side of the mandate. In that context, risk management discipline around macro event risk becomes as important as stock selection in driving total returns across equity portfolios. market_summary: U.S. equities saw sharp factor and sector rotation as a blowout payroll report, hotter inflation data, and Middle East-driven oil volatility whipsawed risk sentiment. Large-cap benchmarks pulled back from recent highs, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq correcting after a multi-week AI-led melt-up, while cyclicals, energy, and select industrials showed relative resilience. Software, unprofitable growth, and crypto-levered names sold off hard, even as semiconductors bifurcated between AI hardware beneficiaries and higher-multiple laggards. Into the next leg, the market is focused on whether strong earnings and AI capex can offset the drag from higher-for-longer rates, elevated oil, and rising geopolitical risk ahead of key inflation data and index rebalancing.

key_trends.theme: AI leadership, but more selective breadth
key_trends.summary: AI remains the primary equity leadership driver, but the market is rotating within the theme. High-quality infrastructure and hardware names are still being rewarded while richly valued software and tools are seeing multiple compression. Investors are increasingly discriminating between durable cash-generators and long-duration stories as rates stay elevated.

key_trends.summary: A stronger labor market, upside inflation surprises, and renewed Middle East tensions have pushed real yields higher and reawakened concerns about a more hawkish Fed path.
